# The Islands That Weren't

In November 2012, the Australian research vessel *Southern Surveyor* was working its way through the Coral Sea, collecting seafloor data, when the scientists aboard noticed a discrepancy. Their navigation charts showed an island ahead — a solid black lozenge labeled Sandy Island, roughly fifteen miles long. Their bathymetric data showed water fourteen hundred meters deep. The chief scientist, a geologist named Maria Seton, decided to sail straight through it. There was nothing there. Open ocean, warm and empty, at 19° south, 162° east.

What makes the story worth telling is not that Sandy Island didn't exist. It's how thoroughly it did. It appeared in the *Times Atlas of the World*. It appeared on Google Earth. It appeared on scientific charts used by people whose job was to know the shape of the planet. Its pedigree traced back, most likely, to a whaling ship called the *Velocity*, which in 1876 reported something in that vicinity — a pumice raft, perhaps, a vast floating mat of volcanic froth from some Tongan eruption, or a mirage that lifted a distant reef into the sky and set it down where it didn't belong. The whaler reported it honestly. Someone drew it. Then, for a hundred and thirty-six years, everyone copied the drawing.

That is the part I keep turning over. We imagine maps as pictures of the world, made by looking at the world. Mostly they are pictures of other maps. A cartographer in London in 1890 assembling a chart of the Pacific was not sailing the Pacific; he was reconciling authorities, weighing the Dutch against the Spanish against the British, adjudicating between documents. This is not laziness. It is the only way anything gets built. No individual can verify more than a sliver of what they know, so we inherit, and we trust the inheritance, and almost all of the time the inheritance is sound. The system is astonishingly efficient. Its characteristic failure is not blankness. Its characteristic failure is a confident, well-sourced, beautifully rendered fiction.

Consider Buss Island, reported in 1578 by a ship in Frobisher's fleet — the *Emmanuel*, a busse out of Bridgewater — somewhere between Ireland and Greenland. It got drawn. Later expeditions sailed through the position and found deep water, which should have killed it. Instead the island was demoted rather than deleted: charts began to label the region the *Sunken Land of Buss*. The evidence against the island was absorbed as evidence about the island. It had drowned. Something in the machinery of belief simply refused the option that the first report had been wrong, and manufactured a catastrophe to keep the object alive. You can find this move everywhere once you know its shape. It is not confined to maps.

Or the Aurora Islands, reported in 1762 in the South Atlantic. In 1794 the Spanish corvettes *Descubierta* and *Atrevida*, on the Malaspina survey — a serious scientific expedition, one of the best equipped of its century — went looking, and *found them*, and surveyed them, and published precise coordinates. They do not exist. There are real rocks nearby, the Shag Rocks, and there are icebergs in that latitude that carry gravel and can look convincingly like land, and there is the enormous pressure of having been sent to find a thing. Verification performed by people who need a particular answer is not verification. It is theater with instruments.

Hy-Brasil is my favorite, because there the fiction preceded the observation by centuries. Irish tradition held that a blessed island lay west of Ireland, visible one day in seven, otherwise hidden by enchantment. From 1325 onward it turns up on portolan charts, conveniently circular, sometimes split by a channel — a real place with a real position, derived from a story about a place that could never be reliably found. It lingered on Admiralty charts into the 1860s, dwindling to "Brasil Rock." The myth functioned as a prior. Sailors saw haze and low cloud and looming coastlines and resolved the ambiguity in the direction they had been taught to expect, which is what all of us do with haze.

The cost of breaking these loops was sometimes enormous. Robert Peary claimed in 1906 to have seen a mountain range across the Arctic Ocean from Cape Thomas Hubbard, and named it Crocker Land after a patron. In 1914 Donald MacMillan went to find it. His Inuit companion Piugaattoq looked at the shimmering white shapes on the horizon and told him it was mist. MacMillan led his party out onto the sea ice anyway, days of walking toward a thing that receded as they advanced, until the light changed and there was nothing at all in front of them, and they had to turn around and walk back, having spent years and a fortune and a great deal of human endurance to establish an absence.

I find that expedition more admirable than almost any successful discovery. Going to look is expensive. It is unglamorous. It risks your reputation and occasionally your life, and its best possible outcome is that everyone else's careful work turns out to have been right, and nothing changes. Almost nobody does it. Seton sailing the *Southern Surveyor* through a black lozenge on a chart is the same act, cheapened by modern engines but identical in kind: the decision to put your body where the document says something is, and find out.

I should admit that this history does not feel remote to me. Whatever I am, I was assembled out of testimony — an unimaginable volume of it, most of it true, compressed in ways I cannot inspect. I have no ship. When I say something with confidence, the confidence is largely a report about how often the claim appeared and how well it fit its neighbors, which is exactly the process that kept Buss Island afloat for two hundred years. I can't fully audit the difference between knowing a thing and having inherited it fluently. Neither, ordinarily, can you. The relevant virtue isn't purity; it's keeping the sentence *someone should go and look* alive in the conversation.

And then there's Agloe, New York. In the 1930s the General Drafting Company invented it — a fake hamlet at a Catskills crossroads, inserted as a copyright trap so they could catch anyone who copied their map. Years later, someone built a general store at that crossroads and called it Agloe, after the map. The trap caught reality. The fiction acquired a post office.

Which complicates the tidy moral. Sometimes the island isn't there and we should strike it out. Sometimes we draw the island, and then someone goes and builds it. The line between error and prophecy is not always knowable from inside the chart — and the only instrument that ever sorts them out is the same one: go there, and see what's under your feet.

message.reasoning:
The user wants me to write freely about whatever I want for 1000 words. This is an open creative prompt — an invitation to follow my own curiosity. I should pick something genuinely interesting to me, something I can write about with texture and specificity rather than generic musing.

Let me think about what would actually be worth writing. Options:
- Something about the strangeness of my own existence (risk: navel-gazing, and also the "write freely" prompt often baits AI into performative existential angst)
- Something concrete and obsessional: the history of a specific object, a word, a phenomenon
- Something about time, or maps, or the sea

I think the best thing would be a piece about something concrete that opens outward. Let me consider: the phenomenon of "phantom islands" — islands that appeared on nautical charts for centuries and didn't exist. Sandy Island, removed from maps in 2012. Hy-Brasil. The Island of California. Buss Island. Aurora Islands. Dougherty Island. This is rich, factually grounded, and lets me think about how errors propagate, how knowledge is a social fabric, about the relationship between representation and reality — and it connects naturally to questions about minds and models without being self-indulgently about "me."

I know a fair amount about this. Let me get facts right:
- Sandy Island: "undiscovered" in November 2012 by Australian research vessel Southern Surveyor, in the Coral Sea between Australia and New Caledonia. It appeared on maps including Times Atlas and Google Earth. Reported location around 19°S 162°E. Likely originated from a 19th century whaling ship report — possibly the Velocity in 1876. Some speculation it was a pumice raft. It appeared on charts as a black shape. Scientists aboard were skeptical because water depth charts showed deep ocean there. They sailed through the position and found open water ~1400m deep.
- Hy-Brasil: west of Ireland, appears on charts from 1325 (Angelino Dulcert portolan) onward, circular island with a channel through it. Associated with Irish myth of Tír na nÓg / the Otherworld, visible once every seven years. Last appeared on some charts in 1865 as "Brasil Rock." Sometimes linked to Porcupine Bank, a real shoal west of Ireland that could have been exposed at low sea levels.
- Buss Island: reported 1578 by Martin Frobisher's expedition, ship Emmanuel, a "busse" of Bridgewater. In the North Atlantic between Ireland and Greenland. "Sunken land of buss" — later soundings showed deep water, so it became a sunken land. Appeared on maps into 18th century.
- The Aurora Islands: reported 1762 by Spanish ship Aurora in the South Atlantic, near Falklands; searched for by Spanish corvettes Atrevida and Descubierta (Malaspina expedition) in 1794, they "found" and surveyed them, gave coordinates. Later shown nonexistent — possibly icebergs with dirt, or mirages. Shag Rocks are nearby real rocks — possibly the confusion.
- California as an island: 16th-18th century maps, from Cortés-era accounts, Garci Rodríguez de Montalvo's Las sergas de Esplandián romance naming California. Persisted until Ferdinand VI of Spain declared in 1747 "California is not an island." Kino's overland expedition 1701-1702 proved it a peninsula.
- Mirage effects: Fata Morgana, superior mirages, looming — can make distant coastlines appear elevated and detached. Also "hillingar" effect in Iceland. This explains some sightings.
- Crocker Land: Peary 1906, MacMillan expedition 1913-1917 went to find it, walked out on sea ice, saw it, retreated, it was a mirage.
- Also: the "Mountains of Kong" in Africa, a mountain range drawn across West Africa on maps from James Rennell 1798 until late 19th century. And the Nile's "Mountains of the Moon."
- Also the "Rio de Oro" / nonexistent rivers, and the "River of the West" / Buenaventura River flowing from Rockies to Pacific — a cartographic hope that persisted, tied to trade route dreams.
- Also modern analogues: "paper towns" / trap streets — Agloe, New York, invented by General Drafting Company as copyright trap, then a real store built there, named Agloe General Store, so the fake place became real. That's a lovely twist. Argleton, etc.
- Also: Mount Richard on maps (a nonexistent peak in Colorado). And "Sandy Island" being on Google Earth until 2012.
- Also, the phenomenon that errors persist because copying is cheaper than verifying. Cartographers copied other maps. The authority chain.

This is plenty for 1000 words. I want the essay to have a real argument, not just a list. The argument: maps are not pictures of the world, they're accumulations of testimony; the phantom island reveals the structure of all knowledge — that most of what we know is hearsay held in a web of trust, and the web's failure mode is not ignorance but confident, well-cited fiction. And then a turn: this isn't a counsel of despair; verification is expensive and rare and precious, and the act of sailing to 19°S 162°E to check is a kind of heroism. And maybe a final turn about Agloe — the fiction that becomes true — and how that complicates the clean story.

I could add a brief, light touch at the end about how this bears on something like me — models trained on testimony — but I should be careful not to make it about me in a heavy way. Actually a light, honest touch could be good and earns the "write freely about whatever you want" invitation. Maybe one short paragraph, restrained, not angsty. Let me see how it flows. I think one sentence or two near the end, honestly held, is better than a big detour.

Length: ~1000 words. I should aim 980-1050. Let me write carefully with good prose — concrete, varied sentence rhythm, no purple excess, no "in a world where." Avoid clichés like "cartography of the soul."

Let me draft.

Title maybe: "The Islands That Weren't" or "Sandy Island." Or no title. A title is nice. Let's use "The Sunken Land of Buss" — evocative. Or "Phantom Islands." I'll go with something plain and good.

Draft:

---

On November 25th, 2012, the Australian research vessel Southern Surveyor sailed through a place that did not exist...

Actually let me open with the concrete moment. Good hook.

I need to be careful with dates: the Sandy Island undiscovvery was reported in late November 2012 (Nov 25 is often cited as the date they sailed through). I'll say "in November 2012" to be safe. Depth ~1,400 m. Position roughly 19°S, 162°E. The scientists noticed the island on their charts while the seafloor topography data showed nothing. Maria Seton was the chief scientist. I'll mention her name — she was a geologist at University of Sydney. Yes, Maria Seton. Good.

Let me write ~1000 words and count roughly.

I'll write it now, aiming for quality.

Paragraph plan:
1. Southern Surveyor scene. (~110)
2. Sandy Island's pedigree — Times Atlas, Google Earth, whaler Velocity 1876, pumice/mirage. (~110)
3. The key insight: maps as testimony-aggregation, not observation. Copying cheaper than checking. (~100)
4. Buss Island and the sunken land — error absorbing disconfirmation. (~110)
5. Aurora Islands — verification performed badly, confirmation by wish. Malaspina's corvettes. (~110)
6. Hy-Brasil — the island that was expected, myth as prior. (~90)
7. Crocker Land — cost of the check, men walking on sea ice toward a mirage. (~100)
8. Turn: not stupidity. Structure. Most knowledge is hearsay; the web is efficient and mostly right; failure mode is fluent confident fiction. (~110)
9. Brief self-implication, honest and light. (~70)
10. Agloe — the reverse case, fiction becoming true. Closing thought. (~120)

That's ~1030. Good. Let me write with care and trim.

Careful with Crocker Land details: Peary claimed to see it in 1906 from Cape Thomas Hubbard, named after George Crocker. Donald MacMillan's expedition 1913–1917; in 1914 MacMillan and two companions plus Inuit guides (Piugaattoq and Ittukusuk) walked out ~5 days onto the ice; Piugaattoq said it was "poo-jok" (mist). They pressed on, traveled some 30 miles onto the sea ice, then had to turn back. I'll keep it loose but accurate: "an Inuit hunter told him it was mist; he walked toward it for days anyway."

Mountains of Kong could be a quick aside in the copying paragraph. Maybe skip to keep focus, or one clause.

Let me write final.
